title: Optics
tagline: How light travels, bends and interferes
summary: Geometrical optics of mirrors and lenses, then the wave theory: interference, diffraction and polarisation.
overview: Geometrical optics treats light as rays that reflect and refract. It is an approximation, valid when obstacles are large compared with a wavelength, and it is good enough to design a telescope. The wave theory is the more fundamental account: light is the electromagnetic wave of the magnetism course, and rays are the direction in which the wave’s energy travels.

The first chapter covers reflection, refraction, the thin-lens equation and optical instruments, with the sign convention stated explicitly. Interference and diffraction then explain what rays cannot: why a double slit produces fringes, why a single slit has a width, and why a grating disperses colours. Polarisation is the evidence that the wave is transverse.

Path difference, not a memorised formula, is the thing to compute. A bright fringe is a path difference of a whole number of wavelengths, once any phase change on reflection has been counted. The small-angle approximation sin θ ≈ tan θ ≈ θ (in radians) is used constantly and should be labelled when it is used.
outcomes: Apply the law of reflection and Snell’s law, including total internal reflection.
Use the mirror and thin-lens equations with a consistent sign convention, and locate images.
Explain two-slit interference and thin-film interference in terms of path difference.
Find the single-slit diffraction pattern and the resolving power of a circular aperture.
Use the grating equation and describe how a spectrometer separates wavelengths.
Account for polarisation by selective absorption, reflection and birefringence, and use Malus’s law.

history.title: The sine law of refraction
history.detail: Willebrord Snell found that the sines of the angles of incidence and refraction are in a constant ratio. Descartes published the law in 1637.

history.title: Newton’s Opticks
history.detail: Newton’s Opticks set out experiments on the prism, thin films (Newton’s rings) and diffraction, and defended a particle theory of light.

history.title: Young’s interference
history.detail: Thomas Young’s lectures of 1801–1803 showed that light from two slits forms fringes, which a particle picture does not explain.

history.title: Fresnel’s memoir
history.detail: Augustin-Jean Fresnel’s memoir on diffraction, assessed by Poisson and Arago, predicted the bright spot in the shadow of a disc and confirmed the wave theory.

history.title: Polarisation by reflection
history.detail: Étienne-Louis Malus found that light reflected from glass at a particular angle is polarised, evidence that the light wave is transverse.

history.title: Light as an electromagnetic wave
history.detail: Maxwell’s identification of light with an electromagnetic disturbance explains why the wave is transverse and why its speed is 1/√(ε₀μ₀).
